place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 外门 · 大通铺
place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the long dormitory bed

setup.zh: 腊月初八的黄昏。观主把玉盒子放在祁长松手里；你是伙房大娘拿晾衣杆从树上捅下来的。夜里，周衡结「另议」那一笔；阿禾押的那一文，输了。
setup.en: Dusk on the eighth of the twelfth month. The abbot sets the jade box in Qi Changsong's hands; you are poked down out of the tree by the kitchen auntie with a clothes pole. At night Zhou Heng settles the 'to be settled'; the one cash A He bet is lost.

recap.zh: 筑基丹归了祁长松；观主说：「前四，进内门名册。」褚先生搭了你的右腕：「掌上那个，不是反噬。」大比那夜，周衡结了巡夜那一笔，十块灵石；阿禾押的一文输了。柴房里，两只破袜子换来一口鸳鸯锅，银月吃上了火锅。孙二狗说：「台上倒了七回，起来了七回。」你给家里写了第一封信：「娘，漏勺也能打水。」夜里银月说，镜子裂的那一下，那头有人：「叫徐州那个，十月去邺城等着。」
recap.en: The Foundation pill went to Qi Changsong; the abbot said: "The last four go into the inner register." Master Chu took your right wrist: "That thing on the palm isn't backlash." The night of the contest Zhou Heng settled the night-watch account — ten stones; the one cash A He bet was lost. In the woodshed two holey socks bought a split hotpot, and Yinyue had her hotpot at last. Sun Ergou said: "Seven times down on the stage, seven times up." You wrote your first letter home: "Ma, a skimmer can carry water too." That night Yinyue said someone was at the other end when the mirror cracked: "Send the one from Xu. Tenth month, to Ye, to wait."

zh: 「叫徐州那个，十月去邺城等着。」
en: "The last four go into the inner register."
"Send the one from Xu. Tenth month, to Ye, to wait."

story.zh:
冠军，筑基丹一枚。观主把那只玉盒子放在祁长松手里，玉盒子玉色青白，盒盖上贴着一道封条，封条上盖着观主的大印；盒子还没打开，一缕清苦的药香已经从缝里渗出来，冷冷的，像腊月清早的松针，前排的人不由自主地吸了一口气，吸完了，胸口里一凉，又一热。祁长松双手接了，跪下，磕了一个头，起来的时候，眼眶是红的。周衡把那本蓝布面的名录摊开，往前翻了几十页，翻到划了一道的那一页，看了一眼，才又翻回来，翻到新的一页，把笔递给了唱名的执事。

小满是伙房大娘拿晾衣杆从树上捅下来的。大娘一面捅，一面念叨：「又是你。」

他落了地，往台下走，人堆自己往两边分开一条道。他走过的地方，没有人笑他，好些人看他，看得很久。观主从竹椅上站起来，走到他跟前，温和地道：「前四，进内门名册。」顿了一顿，又道：「沉鼎秘境里，有一间石室。三百年，没人进去过……」他没说完，拍了拍他的肩膀，转身走了。小满站在那里，后背上的汗，一下子全冒了出来。

马小宝是给两个跟班架回大通铺的，手里还攥着那面裂了的镜子，倒下去的时候也没撒手。他是四强，名册上也添了他，可他一路上一句话也没说，只回过头去，往泗水那边望。马家的船已经开走了。

小满往山门那边望了一眼。瞿老站在台阶上，拄着扫帚，也在看。可瞿老看的不是他，是祁长松手里那只玉盒子。那一眼很长，长得不像是在看一只盒子，倒像是在看一件很多年以前的旧事。然后瞿老转过身去，扫地了。

台阶底下，褚先生在等他。人都往伙房那边散了，老先生一个人站在那里，冲他伸出两根指头：「腕子。」小满把左腕递过去。褚先生不接，道：「那一只。」小满站了一会儿，把右手从袖子里伸了出来。褚先生搭了很久，久到山门那边瞿老的扫帚又响了起来。他把那只手翻过来，看了一眼掌心，又翻了回去，松了手，道：「脉上是四层，跟名册上一样。」捋了一下山羊胡子，转身走了，走出去三步，头也不回，又补了一句：「掌上那个，不是反噬。」

天黑下来的时候，周衡在执事房里点上了那半根蜡烛。小满进去的时候，他已经翻开了巡夜簿，拿指头点着一行一行往下念：「十月初一至初九，药园丢灵草十株。初八起，沈小满巡夜；初十以后，一株没丢，外加灵兽一只，狰，入册。另议的那一笔，今天议——」他从抽屉里一块一块地往外数，「——一、二、三……十块。」

小满看着那十块灵石，没有伸手。周衡道：「腊八结账，结在晚上。」他把账簿合上，难得多说了一句：「《礼记》上说，古时候天子年底祭『蜡』，连吃田鼠的猫都请来谢。用过人家的，一定要还。连猫的账，都结。」小满把灵石揣进怀里，走到门口，回过头来叫了一声：「……周师兄。」周衡道：「嗯。」小满说：「有前途。」周衡咳嗽一声，耳朵根「腾」地红了，算盘珠子拨错了两颗，挥挥手，叫他滚了。

钱掌柜在老槐树底下收摊，算盘还没收进袖子，看见阿禾过来，抬起眼皮。阿禾把那张折成一小块的纸条打开，摊在秤盘上，面无表情：「掌柜的，我押的那一文，输了。」钱掌柜道：「输了。」阿禾道：「纸条还你。」钱掌柜收了纸条，那一文钱，早在他布袋里了。阿禾站了一站，从怀里摸出小本子，翻开，拿炭条一笔一笔地写，写完了，合上，转身走了。

他站在老槐树底下，先是笑，笑出了声，笑得肋下那根骨头一抽一抽地疼；笑着笑着，眼睛便热了，热得看不清那棵槐树。他拿那只烙了印的手背揩了揩眼睛，揩完了，还在笑。那一文钱，是她娘缝在她衣角里的，初七那天她拿剪子挑开了线。阿禾走出去几步，回过头来，看了他一眼，道：「你今天没藏。」小满没说话，右手攥着，没有张开。她只说了两个字：「藏好。」

那天夜里，柴房的门闩上了，柴墩上支起了伙房大娘借给他的一口豁了边的铁锅。那罐牛脂甘露，早上全洒在了冻地上，伙房门口那一片，这时候还是香的。可十月里那一罐是拿什么换的，小满记得：一只破袜子。他把自己脚上那两只脱了下来——补了又补，前头露着两个脚趾头——一只一只丢进了饭桶，送了两口灵气。周衡给的十块灵石揣在怀里，他一块也没动。「咯嘣」，「咯嘣」，「咔哒」。肚里躺着一块方方正正的锅底，凝着油，当中一道隔，一半红得发亮，一半清得见底。

锅一滚，花椒味冲得小狰连打了三个喷嚏。锅底下垫的是那撮自己打转的土，锅搁上去，便慢慢地转，转到谁跟前，谁下筷子。孙二狗是他拉来的，捧着一只碗，看着那口自己转圈的锅，半天没敢动。木牌一烫，银月钻了出来，蹲在锅沿上，两只前爪举过头顶：「今晚火锅——耶～～」那一声，只小满听得见。她吃得极快：孙二狗夹起一片腊肉，吹了三口，低头一看，筷子上空了；锅里的豆腐，眼看着一块一块少下去。孙二狗揉了揉眼睛，看看锅，看看小满，小声道：「沈师兄，这锅……漏？」小满道：「漏。」银月拿那根牙签——饭桶头一回吐的那一根——剔了剔牙，剔完了，又拿它串了三块豆腐。那粒更小的石子，小满拿来架筷子。孙二狗从红的那半边捞上来一块锅巴，煮了一晚上，还是硬的，一口咬下去，「咯嘣」一声，捂着腮帮子半天说不出话——葛六捏得碎核桃，捏不碎这个。小满弯腰添柴，腰带夹层里滚出一个油纸包，散开了，一颗粉里透红的丸子骨碌碌滚到孙二狗碗边。孙二狗伸手便拿：「这个丸子——」小满和银月一齐扑了过去，小满抢在手里，塞进了储物袋：「……那个，不是丸子。」

吃到后来，锅里只剩两半汤。银月仰面躺在锅沿上，肚皮滚圆，拿牙签剔着牙，懒懒地道：「这锅底不坏。哪家铺子的？」小满道：「袜子。」银月的牙签停在了半空。她低头看看自己的肚皮，又看看小满光着的两只脚，「呕」了一声，什么也没呕出来，钻回了木牌。小满没理她。他看着柴垛底下那只饭桶，在肚里过了一遍：柴火棍换牙签，石子换更小的石子，窝头换锅巴，墙根土换一撮自己打转的土，一根残株换九道纹的回春丹，两块灵石换一颗含笑半步颠；一只袜子换一罐，两只袜子，换两半。它不是乱吐的——喂什么，喂多少，喂的什么成色，便吐什么。这笔账，他没处写，记在了肚子里。

这一夜，伙房里，通铺上，内门的廊下，说的都是一件事。外门三十年没出过冠军，这一回也没出；可一个四层的外门弟子，把内门的卢方扔下了台，把秦雁打了下去，把马小宝的镜子照裂了，末了，叫祁不退退了一步。「他凭什么？」「运气。」「运气能连着撞上四回？」大通铺上，马小宝裹着被子，在火盆边上抖了半夜，牙齿磕着牙齿，只说了一句：「镜子照着他……他手底下，亮了。」没人听懂，也没人理他。

那天夜里，人都睡下了以后，孙二狗摸到了小满的铺位跟前，蹲了好一会儿，才小声道：「沈师兄。卢师兄那一脚……你替我还了。」小满道：「他自己踩空的。」孙二狗道：「五行台上的石头，是干的。」小满道：「风大。」孙二狗便不说话了。他从腰里解下那个蓝布包，断了的那根绳子，他已经拿线接上了，那只肿手使不上劲，接得歪歪扭扭。他道：「沈师兄，我今天……倒了七回。我娘说，人倒了不丢人，倒了不起来才丢人。」他咧嘴笑了一下，扯着下巴上的伤，嘶了一口气，「台上倒了七回，起来了七回。下了台，在石阶上坐下去那一回……我是真起不来了。是你拉的。」小满没有说话。黑暗里，他听见孙二狗摸回了自己的铺位，躺下去的时候，还小声地念叨了一句：「……记着了。」隔了一会儿，黑地里又传来他的声音：「沈师兄，你会写字吧？」小满道：「会几个。」孙二狗道：「明天……你替我写一封信。我娘不识字，村里有个先生会念。你就写：娘，我倒了七回，起来了七回。」他顿了一顿，「别写是谁把我打倒的。」
story.en:
Champion: one Foundation pill. The abbot set the jade box in Qi Changsong's hands — bluish-white jade, a seal strip across its lid stamped with the abbot's great seal; before it was even opened a thread of clean bitter scent seeped from the seam, cold, like pine needles on a twelfth-month dawn, and the front row drew breath without meaning to, and felt their chests go cool, then warm. Qi Changsong took it in both hands, knelt, and knocked his head once on the ground, and when he rose his eyes were red. Zhou Heng spread open the blue register, turned back dozens of pages to the one with the stroke through it, looked once, then turned forward again to a new page and handed the brush to the steward who called the names.

Xiaoman was poked down out of the tree by the kitchen auntie with a clothes pole. She muttered as she poked: "You again."

He landed and walked off the stage, and the crowd parted of itself to let him through. Where he passed nobody laughed at him; plenty of them looked at him, and looked a long time. The abbot rose from his bamboo chair, came over to him, and said mildly: "The last four go into the inner register." He paused, then: "In the Chending hidden realm there is a stone chamber. For three hundred years, no one has gone in…" He didn't finish; he patted his shoulder, turned, and walked away. Xiaoman stood there, and the sweat broke out all down his back.

Ma Xiaobao was carried back to the bunkhouse between two followers, still clutching the cracked mirror; he hadn't let go of it even when he fell. He was one of the four, and his name went into the register too, but all the way back he said not a word; he only turned his head and looked toward the Si. The Ma boat had already sailed.

Xiaoman looked toward the gate. Elder Qu stood on the steps leaning on his broom, looking too. But he wasn't looking at Xiaoman; he was looking at the jade box in Qi Changsong's hands. A long look, not like looking at a box, more like looking at something that happened many years ago. Then Elder Qu turned away and swept.

At the foot of the steps Master Chu was waiting for him. Everyone had drifted off toward the kitchen; the old teacher stood there alone and held out two fingers: "Your wrist." Xiaoman offered his left. Chu didn't take it: "The other one." Xiaoman stood a moment, then brought his right hand out of his sleeve. Chu held it a long time, so long that over at the gate Elder Qu's broom began to sweep again. He turned the hand over, looked once at the palm, turned it back, and let go: "The pulse says layer four, same as the register." He stroked his goatee, turned and walked away, and three steps on, without looking back, added: "That thing on the palm isn't backlash."

At nightfall Zhou Heng lit the half candle in the stewards' office. When Xiaoman came in he already had the night-watch book open and was reading down it line by line with a finger: "First to ninth of the tenth month, ten herbs lost from the garden. From the eighth, Shen Xiaoman on night watch; after the tenth, not one lost, plus one spirit beast, a zheng, entered in the register. The 'to be settled' — settled today." He counted stones out of the drawer one by one, "— one, two, three… ten."

Xiaoman looked at the ten stones and didn't reach for them. "Laba accounts close in the evening," said Zhou Heng. He shut the ledger and, for once, said one thing more: "The Book of Rites says that at year's end the Son of Heaven held the Zha rite and thanked even the cats that ate the field mice. What you've used of someone else's, you must pay back. Even the cats' accounts are settled." Xiaoman tucked the stones into his coat, went to the door, and turned back. "…Brother Zhou." "Mm." "You've got a future." Zhou Heng coughed, his ears went red to the roots, two abacus beads slipped the wrong way, and he waved him out.

Money-Keeper Qian was packing up his stall under the old pagoda tree, abacus not yet back in his sleeve, when he saw A He coming and raised his eyelids. A He unfolded the slip of paper she'd folded small and spread it on the scale pan, deadpan: "Shopkeeper, the one cash I bet — lost." "Lost," said Qian. "Here's your slip back." Qian took the slip; the cash had long since gone into his bag. A He stood a moment, took out her little notebook, opened it, wrote stroke by stroke in charcoal, shut it, turned, and walked off.

He stood under the pagoda tree and laughed first, laughed out loud, laughed till the rib jerked with pain; and laughing, his eyes went hot, so hot he couldn't see the tree. He wiped his eyes with the back of his branded hand, and when he'd wiped them he was still laughing. That one cash her mother had sewn into her hem; on the seventh she'd snipped the thread. A He went a few steps, looked back at him, and said: "You didn't hide today." Xiaoman said nothing; his right hand stayed closed. She said just two words: "Hide well."

That night the woodshed door was barred, and on the chopping block stood an iron pot with a chipped rim, lent him by the kitchen auntie. The jar of Beef-Tallow Nectar had all gone over the frozen yard that morning; the ground by the kitchen door still smelled of it. But what that jar had been traded for in the tenth month, Xiaoman remembered: one holey sock. He pulled off the two on his own feet — darned and darned again, two toes poking through at the front — dropped them into the Rice Tub one at a time, and gave it two mouthfuls of qi. The ten spirit stones Zhou Heng had paid him stayed in his coat, untouched. *Crunch*, *crunch*, *click*. In its belly lay a square cake of hotpot base, set in its fat, a divider down the middle: one half glossy red, one half clear to the bottom.

When the pot boiled, the pepper smell made the zheng sneeze three times running. Under the pot he'd set the pinch of earth that turned by itself; with the pot on it, it slowly revolved, and whoever it came round to took a turn with the chopsticks. Sun Ergou, whom he'd dragged along, held a bowl and stared at the pot going round and round, and for a long while didn't dare move. The token burned, and Yinyue popped out, squatted on the rim, and raised both forepaws over her head: "Hotpot tonight — yay~~" Only Xiaoman could hear it. She ate very fast: Sun Ergou picked up a slice of cured pork, blew on it three times, looked down — his chopsticks were empty; the tofu in the pot was going, piece by piece, before his eyes. Sun Ergou rubbed his eyes, looked at the pot, looked at Xiaoman, and whispered: "Brother Shen, does this pot… leak?" "It leaks," said Xiaoman. Yinyue picked her teeth with the toothpick — the first thing the Tub ever spat out — and when she was done, skewered three pieces of tofu on it. The even smaller pebble Xiaoman used as a chopstick rest. Sun Ergou fished a lump of crust out of the red half — boiled all evening, still hard — bit down — *crack* — and held his cheek a long while without a word: Ge Liu could crack walnuts with two fingers, but not this. Xiaoman bent to add wood, and an oilpaper packet rolled out of his belt fold and came open, and a pink pill rolled up against Sun Ergou's bowl. Sun Ergou reached for it: "This meatball —" Xiaoman and Yinyue lunged at once; Xiaoman got it, and stuffed it into his storage pouch. "…That's not a meatball."

By the end there were only two halves of broth left. Yinyue lay on her back on the rim, belly round as a drum, picking her teeth, and said lazily: "Not a bad base. Which shop's?" "Socks," said Xiaoman. The toothpick stopped in midair. She looked down at her belly, then at Xiaoman's two bare feet, and retched — nothing came up — and went back into the token. Xiaoman paid her no mind. He looked at the Rice Tub under the woodpile and went over it in his head: a stick of firewood for a toothpick, a pebble for a smaller pebble, half a bun for a crust, a handful of wall-foot earth for a pinch of earth that turns by itself, a herb stub for a nine-line Spring-Return pill, two spirit stones for a Smiling Half-Step Topple; one sock for one jar, two socks for two halves. It didn't spit at random — what you fed it, how much, and of what grade, that was what came out. He had nowhere to write the account; he kept it in his belly.

That night, in the kitchen, on the bunks, in the inner court's corridors, there was only one story. The outer court hadn't had a champion in thirty years, and still didn't; but an outer disciple at layer four had thrown the inner court's Lu Fang off the stage, knocked Qin Yan down, shone Ma Xiaobao's mirror back at him till it cracked, and at the end made Never-Back Qi take a step back. "How did he do it?" "Luck." "Luck four times running?" On the big bunk Ma Xiaobao shook half the night in his quilt by the brazier, teeth knocking, and said only one thing: "The mirror shone on him… under his hand, it lit up." No one understood, and no one paid him any mind.

That night, when everyone was asleep, Sun Ergou crept to Xiaoman's bunk and crouched a long while before he whispered: "Brother Shen. Brother Lu's stamp… you paid it back for me." "He missed his own footing." "The stones on the platform are dry." "It was windy." Sun Ergou said no more. He untied the blue pouch; the snapped string he'd already mended with thread, crooked, his swollen hand had no strength in it. "Brother Shen, today I… fell seven times. Ma says falling down's no shame; not getting up is." He grinned, pulled at the cut on his chin, and hissed. "Seven times down on the stage, seven times up. Off the stage, when I sat on the steps… I really couldn't get up. You pulled me." Xiaoman said nothing. In the dark he heard Sun Ergou feel his way back to his bunk, and as he lay down he murmured: "…I'll remember." After a while his voice came again out of the dark: "Brother Shen, you can write, can't you?" "A few words." "Tomorrow… write a letter for me. My ma can't read; there's a teacher in the village who'll read it to her. Just write: Ma, I fell seven times, and got up seven times." A pause. "Don't write who knocked me down."

exits.means: rests, ends the day, or asks what comes next

story.zh:
孙二狗走了以后，小满趴在铺上，就着窗外的月光，给家里写第一封信。他头一句写的是「娘，我当上仙人了」，擦了；第二句写「娘，我打赢了马小宝」，想了想，这话要是传到村里，马三怕是要上门，又擦了。

小满在铺上一笔一笔地写：**娘：我进仙门了。一年五两，观里说腊月就送到家。屋顶修一修。盆可以收起来了，十七个都收。给我爹买一副护膝，狗皮的。给吴婆婆，再送一条鹿腿，这回是买的。我在这里很好。有人欺负我，我记着账。有几笔，已经还上了。——小满**

握笔的是右手。月光底下，那个圈里一横贴着笔杆，凉凉的。他写完了，把那只手翻过来看了一会儿，又翻了回去。

小满把信折好，想了想，又打开来，在最底下添了一行：**娘，漏勺也能打水。**信压在枕头底下，明天一早交给周衡，跟沈家那一包五两银子一车送下山。弓就搁在枕头边上，他伸手摸了摸那十七道牛筋。他握着胸口的木牌，小声道：「你欠我的那张饼……还欠着吧？」木牌轻轻地，烫了一下。像是在说：**还欠着。**

隔了一会儿，木牌又烫了一下，这一回烫得发紧。银月的声音很低，一点也不懒：「镜子裂的那一下，镜子那头，有人。」小满一下子坐了起来：「哪头？」银月道：「很远。西边。本王只听见一句。」她顿了一顿，学那个声音，学得很平，平得没有一点起伏：「叫徐州那个，十月去邺城等着。」

小满在黑地里坐了很久。镜子裂的时候，镜子跟前站着的只有他一个；那道光往他胸口钻，钻着找的是木牌。徐州那个，就是他。他把右手翻过来，掌心那个圈里一横，凉凉的。邺城在哪里，他不知道。他心想：这一句，记住了。
story.en:
When Sun Ergou had gone, Xiaoman lay on his bunk and by the moonlight at the window wrote his first letter home. The first line he wrote was "Ma, I've become an immortal" — rubbed out; the second, "Ma, I beat Ma Xiaobao" — he thought, if that got back to the village Ma San might come round, and rubbed it out too.

On his bunk Xiaoman wrote stroke by stroke: **Ma: I've entered the immortals' gate. Five taels a year; the temple says it'll reach home in the twelfth month. Fix the roof. The basins can be put away — all seventeen. Buy Pa a pair of kneepads, dog-skin. Send Granny Wu another leg of venison — bought, this time. I'm fine here. When people bully me, I keep accounts. A few are paid already. — Xiaoman**

He wrote with his right hand. In the moonlight the circle with its bar lay against the brush, cold. When he had finished he turned the hand over and looked at it a while, then turned it back.

Xiaoman folded the letter, thought, opened it again and added one line at the bottom: **Ma, a skimmer can carry water too.** He tucked it under his pillow; in the morning it would go to Zhou Heng and down the mountain on the same cart as the Shen family's five taels. The bow lay beside his pillow; he reached out and touched its seventeen wraps of sinew. Holding the token on his chest, he whispered: "That flatbread you owe me… still owed, right?" The token warmed, very lightly. As if to say: **Still owed.**

After a while the token burned again, tight this time. Yinyue's voice was low and not lazy at all: "The moment the mirror cracked — there was someone at the other end of it." Xiaoman sat straight up. "Which end?" "Far. West. I caught only one line." She paused, and copied the voice, very level, without a rise or fall in it: "Send the one from Xu. Tenth month, to Ye, to wait."

Xiaoman sat a long time in the dark. When the mirror cracked, he was the only one standing before it; the light had bored into his chest, and what it was looking for was the token. The one from Xu was him. He turned his right hand over: the ring with a bar across it in his palm, cool. Where Ye was, he didn't know. He thought: that line — I'll remember it.
